The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC:      
Objective for processing: 
The purpose of this request for data is to contribute towards improving the evidence base underpinning NHS commissioning of cost-effective neurological rehabilitation services for children with acquired brain injury (ABI).
Paediatric ABI is a major cause of long term morbidity. Rehabilitation services are the mainstay of the response to ABI. However, despite their central role, they are poorly understood and the evidence base to support their effectiveness is weak. Basic incidence data for various causes of paediatric ABI are available, but details of subsequent morbidity patterns are lacking. This hampers estimation of population rehabilitation service needs and understanding of the most effective way of providing rehabilitation services to children who suffer an ABI.
It has been estimated that 800-900 children survive an ABI with significant physical disability requiring physical rehabilitation annually in the UK. In addition a much larger population of survivors of brain injury resulting from trauma, with cognitive and behavioural morbidity, exists. These individuals are over-represented in child and adolescent mental health services and in the offender population. It is acknowledged that inadequate rehabilitation care after a brain injury undermines effective acute care in terms of long term health outcomes, yet little is known about how best to provide paediatric rehabilitation services. 
The first stage of this work is funded by an NIHR Programme Development Grant. The data that is  requested from HSCIC is needed to inform an application for a future NIHR Programme Grant. No systematic picture exists of UK paediatric rehabilitation providers or patient flows. The extent to which rehabilitation for children who suffer an ABI currently occurs in secondary settings is not known. The data requested from HSCIC is to provide a current picture of the epidemiology of paediatric ABI in England and of patient flows through acute and secondary services.
All work will be undertaken within the UK..
The target date for completing this phase of the project is March 2016
Data provided for this phase will not be used in any further phases. Any subsequent phases requiring data will be subject to a new application for data.

Processing activities: 
The HSCIC will supply filtered pseudonymised HES data which will identify paediatric (aged 1-18 years) admissions  that have an ICD-10 code that indicates possible ABI. A&E data linked to the filtered admitted patient care will also be supplied to track patient pathway from A&E to an inpatient. 
The building where the work will be done is a Newcastle University building  and on the Royal Victoria Infirmary site. The data will be stored securely within the University on a standalone computer with no external or internet connection.  Data will be deleted and destroyed after analysis is complete.
National data from 2007 is requested to enable a study of geographic variation in patterns of length of stay to allow sufficient follow-up time from an initial ABI-related admission to subsequent contact with rehabilitation services.
The data will not be linked to any other datasets

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
The primary output from this piece of work will be an understanding of the epidemiology of paediatric ABI and of patient flows through services, which will inform the development of an application for a future  National Institute of Health Research Programme Grant to fund phase 2 of the project. Any change in purpose or where additional data is required for phase 2 will be applied for as part of a new application.  It is anticipated that this piece of work will be completed by March 2016. 
The data on the epidemiology and patient flow of paediatric ABI will be written up for publication in a peer-reviewed journal (estimated date of submission March 2016). All data will be presented in aggregated form, so that it will not be possible for individuals to be identified from any published work ( with data suppressed in line with HES Analyis Guide).
This analysis is to identify centres with differing approaches/pathways for paediatric rehabilitation that can be studied in more detail in a planned subsequent full Programme Grant under the NIHR Programme Grants for Applied Research (PGfAR) scheme, and to inform the planning of the cohort study central to the planned full programme. There is an expectation from NIHR that findings of sufficient robustness, quality, originality and significance will also be published in the peer-reviewed Programme Grants for Applied Research Journal in the NIHR Journals Library. Additional papers reporting specific aspects of the work may be submitted to more specialist journals: for example the results of this analysis may be of interest to Archives of Disease in Childhood, Child Health Care and Development or similar specialist paediatric journals.
No commercial use will be made of the data.

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
The work proposed here is necessary to inform a larger piece of work (to be submitted as an National Institute of Health Research Programme Grant), which will provide a thorough evaluation of outcomes currently achieved after paediatric ABI in a range of models of care operating within England. This work, in turn, will facilitate the development of an optimal strategy for commissioning of paediatric rehabilitation services to be developed, which will help to ensure a whole pathway approach to rehabilitation, grounded in evidence of the most effective model for providing paediatric rehabilitation to ensure optimal health outcomes.
The target date for completing this phase of the project is March 2016.
The data provided is required for the first phase of the study only. It is vital to the design of the second phase but there are no plans to use HES data in that second phase. Should a currently unanticipated need to access HES data arise in the second phase we would make a second application. The second phase comprises a multi-centre cohort observational study of rehabilitation treatment received and severity-adjusted outcomes achieved after paediatric ABI. We need to identify the centres that will be involved in the second phase (these will mainly be regional children’s hospitals). We need to know how many centres to involve, based on estimates of required total sample size (from power calculations) and evidenced estimates of numbers of children each centre sees (from HES data). Additionally we need to recruit centres with different service configurations particularly in relation to the use of other rehabilitation providers such as local district hospitals, and HES data will allow identification of centres with different characteristic patient flow patterns. Finally the findings of this analysis will likely be of intrinsic health-services research value. The epidemiology of paediatric ABI is very poorly defined: in particular rates of disability after ABI (and thus numbers of children requiring rehabilitation provision) are not well evidenced. This data will inform this question directly
